title: Prompt Caching — why switching models makes a turn slow

questions.prompt: You know you will want a different model for a long task. When is the cheapest moment to make the switch?
options: Any time — a switch costs the same whenever you do it
At the start, before the conversation has grown
Right after a long break, when the cache has expired anyway
questions.explanation: A switch forces a full recompute of everything sent so far, so the cost scales with the conversation size — switching early keeps that recompute small. 'After a break' is tempting because the cache is cold regardless, but by then the conversation is long, so the recompute is larger, not free.

questions.prompt: Which of these leaves the cache warm for the next turn?
options: Appending a new message to the conversation
Starting a new session in a different directory
questions.explanation: Appending sits at the end, so the cached prefix is untouched. A model switch, an effort change, and a fresh session in a new directory all change or replace the prefix, so each one recomputes the request.

questions.prompt: You come back from a 40-minute break, change nothing, and send one message. The turn is much slower and more expensive than the last one. What happened?
options: The cache expired during the break, so the whole conversation was reprocessed
Your model was downgraded for inactivity
questions.explanation: The cache survives only a period of inactivity, and every hit resets the timer; a long gap means the next turn misses and reprocesses the prefix. Overload is tempting because it is the usual explanation for slowness, but here the cost moved too — which points at a re-read, not a queue.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the cache is true?
options: It caches each file separately, so editing one file costs nothing
It matches the exact prefix, so changing anything near the front recomputes everything after it
It is shared across all models, so switching models keeps it warm
It never expires while the conversation is open
questions.explanation: The match is on the exact start of the request, which is why ordering content by how often it changes matters, and why a change near the front is expensive. Per-file caching is the tempting wrong answer — it would be convenient, but the mechanism has no per-file granularity.
